title: Symphony engagements and arrangers Dick Hyman, Glenn Osser and Norman Leyden
summary: Wilson lists upcoming dates with symphonies and arrangers who can write for orchestra, since he writes only for jazz bands.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, that's beautiful. Have you done a couple concerts at the symphony orchestras here? I know you'd gotten some arrangements there.

Yes, I did. I have an appearance with the Buffalo Symphony in just a few days on the 10th of January, just a few days from now, and have several appearances lined up later on in -- you'll have to check the calendar, I think there's one in Rochester, New York, and Minneapolis -- the symphony, and I think the Baltimore Symphony is in there, and I think there's one in St. Louis.
Uh huh.

And so far, my repertoire has four arrangements in them done from Dick Hyman, a featured piano in the Symphonic Strings. I hope to get some more; I'd like to -- there's an arranger I like very much named Glenn Osser who's very capable in this sort of thing.
I know him very well.

He did a string date for me years ago, in May '64, and we talked the whole day on the phone, and I walked in the studio just like the string players, and he had the piano part for me to play -- and they played strings and it was just like putting on an old shoe.
Oh, sure.
Because the arrangement fit me so good. Glenn Miller does. Just talking over the phone, long distance phone, we talked 12 arrangements, we talked over the phone. Very capable man.
Oh, absolutely. I know him well.
And then there's another one, too, I'd like to get who is now -- used to be my old conductor at CBS, he used to conduct the Portland Symphony, Norman Leyden.
Oh, yeah.
You remember him?
Sure, I know Norman.

I played some of his arrangements at CBS years ago, you know, and he could do it, too, because he conducted the Boston Pops last summer here, and he did his own Ellington medley that he had orchestrated, and he opened -- I couldn't hear it because I had to come to work here, but I did hear the opening number that he did. He orchestrated Bach's 'Toccata and Fugue' in D minor. You ever hear that, Ted? It was done back in the twenties.

But Norman did it and it sounded just like the real thing. But these are men that I know that can write for a big orchestra, because I couldn't -- I'm used to writing for the alto sax and the tenor sax, the trombone and the trumpet. But those guys, they're writing for the English horn, the oboes, and the flutes and the French horns
and the instruments that play in the tenor clef and the alto clef , the violas, and that. And you know, Dick Hyman knows all that stuff, too.
Oh, he's amazing -- a very talented man.
So I feel very fortunate that I could get started with these four thing that Dick has given me.
I saw him at dinner the other night -- and also ran into Deedee. I was working there. He's a very bright man and he has a great love for you.
Oh yeah, I'm very fond of him, too.
